questions.knowledge_point: Solving a Quadratic Equation When the Solutions Are Irrational
questions.problem: The equation ${a}^{2}+8a=18$ can be written in the form $(a+p)^{2}=q.$ Find $p+q,$ and solve the equation.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we complete the square on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}^{2}+8a & =18 \\ {a}^{2}+2\cdot 4\cdot a & =18 \\ {a}^{2}+2\cdot a\cdot 4+{4}^{2}-{4}^{2} & =18 \\ (a+4)^{2}-{4}^{2} & =18\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we isolate the perfect square:

$$
\begin{aligned}(a+4)^{2}-{4}^{2} & =18 \\ (a+4)^{2}-16 & =18 \\ (a+4)^{2} & =34\end{aligned}
$$

So, $p=4,q=34,$ and $p+q=38.$

Next, we solve the equation using the square-root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}(a+4)^{2} & =34 \\ \sqrt{(a+4)^{2}} & =\sqrt{34} \\ |a+4| & =\sqrt{34} \\ a+4 & =\pm \sqrt{34} \\ a & =-4\pm \sqrt{34}\end{aligned}
$$

provenance.kp_title: Solving a Quadratic Equation When the Solutions Are Irrational

questions.knowledge_point: Expressing a Definite Integral as the Limit of a Left Riemann Sum
questions.problem: What is ${\int }_{2}^{4}3\sqrt{x}\,\text{d}x$ expressed as the limit of a left Riemann sum?
questions.worked_solution:
The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a left Riemann sum as

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{j=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{j})\cdot Δx,
$$

    

where $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}$ and ${x}_{j}=a+jΔx.$

In the definite integral

$$
{\int }_{2}^{4}3\sqrt{x}\,\text{d}x,
$$

the function is $f(x)=3\sqrt{x},$ the lower bound is $a=2,$ and the upper bound is $b=4.$ So, we have

$$
Δx=\frac{4-2}{n}=\frac{2}{n},
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{2}^{4}3\sqrt{x}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{j=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{j})\cdot Δx \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{j=0}^{n-1}[f(2+j\cdot \frac{2}{n})\cdot \frac{2}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{j=0}^{n-1}[f(2+\frac{2j}{n})\cdot \frac{2}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{j=0}^{n-1}[3\sqrt{2+\frac{2j}{n}}\cdot \frac{2}{n}].\end{aligned}
$$

provenance.kp_title: Expressing a Definite Integral as the Limit of a Left Riemann Sum

questions.problem: Which of the following is the graph of $y=\frac{5}{2x}-2?$
questions.worked_solution:
To plot $y=\frac{5}{2x}-2,$ we apply the following steps:

- Take the curve $y=\frac{1}{x}.$

- Then, stretch the result by a scale factor of $\frac{5}{2}$ parallel to the $y$-axis to get the graph of $y=\frac{5}{2x}.$

- Translate it by $2$ units down to get the graph of $y=\frac{5}{2x}-2.$

questions.knowledge_point: Interpreting the Derivative of a Function
questions.problem: Consider an ellipse such that its major axis $a$ can vary while its minor axis is fixed. What is the best interpretation of ${S}^{′}(a)$ if $S$ is the area enclosed by the ellipse?
questions.worked_solution:
The function $S(a)$ gives the area of the ellipse with major axis $a.$ So,

$$
{S}^{′}(a)=\frac{\text{d}S}{\text{d}a}=\frac{\text{Change in }S}{\text{Change in }a}.
$$

Therefore, ${S}^{′}(a)$ is the rate at which the area changes as the major axis changes.

choices.value: The rate at which the area changes as the major axis changes
The major axis of an ellipse with area S
The rate at which the major axis changes as the minor axis changes
The rate at which the perimeter changes as the major axis changes
The area of an ellipse with major axis $a$

answer_fields.correct_value: The rate at which the area changes as the major axis changes

Which of the diagrams above can be the graph of the polynomial $y=-3{x}^{4}+{x}^{3}-4{x}^{2}+4x?$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's call $P(x)$ the given polynomial:

$$
P(x)=-3{x}^{4}+{x}^{3}-4{x}^{2}+4x
$$

The degree $(n=4)$ is even and the leading coefficient $({a}_{4}=-3)$ is negative. Therefore, the polynomial has the following end behavior:

- $P(x)\to -\infty $ as $x\to \infty .$

- $P(x)\to -\infty $ as $x\to -\infty .$

None of the graphs satisfy these conditions.

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating Sums and Scalar Multiplication of Vectors
questions.worked_solution:
To compute $3a+b,$ we just need to perform the required operations with each component separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}3a+b & =3\cdot ⟨-1,3,2⟩+⟨5,1,4⟩ \\  & =⟨-3,9,6⟩+⟨5,1,4⟩ \\  & =⟨2,10,10⟩\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying the Shift Applied to an Exponential Growth Curve
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13978982/assets/319245f467f8512e0fd1d420364a3a88774eda3c9c17c03d4cba6b073c86ad9e.png)

The graph above shows the curve $y={(\frac{13}{6})}^{x}+c.$ Determine the value of $c$ and find the equation of the curve.
questions.worked_solution:
The horizontal asymptote of $y={(\frac{13}{6})}^{x}$ is $y=0.$ The vertical translation $y={(\frac{13}{6})}^{x}+c$ shifts the asymptote to $y=c.$

In the graph above, the horizontal asymptote is $y=-\frac{3}{2}.$ Therefore, $c=-\frac{3}{2}.$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13978982/assets/d8d23cf36bc9fb526c0e6d041b72e6b378638f662b67aae63531c66b4a8cd6c5.png)

The diagram above shows the local minimum and maximum of the function $y=f(x).$ What is the local maximum of $y=-f(x+2)+4?$
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that the graph of $y=-f(x+2)+4$ can be obtained from the graph of $y=f(x)$ by 

- translating it by $2$ units to the left, then

- flipping it across the $x$-axis, and finally

- translating it by $4$ units up.

Since one of these transformations flips the graph across the $x$-axis, the combined transformation maps the local **minimum** of $y=f(x)$ to the local **maximum** of $y=-f(x+2)+4.$ So, we need to find the image of $(1,-4),$ the local minimum of $y=f(x),$ under the transformation. 

To plot $y=-f(x+2)+4,$ we apply the following steps: 

- First, we take the graph $y=f(x)$ that passes through $(1,-4).$

- Then, we translate the graph by $2$ units to the left and get the graph of $y=f(x+2).$ After this transformation, the point $(1,-4)$ will be mapped to the point

$$
(1-2,-4)=(-1,-4).
$$

- Next, we flip the result across the $x$-axis and get the graph of $y=-f(x+2).$ After this transformation, the point $(-1,-4)$ will be mapped to the point

$$
(-1,-1\cdot (-4))=(-1,4).
$$

- Finally, we translate the result by $4$ units up and get the graph of $y=-f(x+2)+4.$ After this transformation, the point $(-1,4)$ will be mapped to the point

$$
(-1,4+4)=(-1,8).
$$

Therefore, the local maximum of $y=-f(x+2)+4$ is $(-1,8).$
